title: What goes in and what can come out
objectives: State the domain and range of a simple function
Read a range from a graph
Use filled and hollow ends on a number line

screens.prose: This machine divides 12 by its input: $f(x) = \dfrac{12}{x}$. The table shows four inputs.
screens.question: What comes out when 0 goes in?

options.why: You took $12 \div 0$ as 0. But $0 \times 0 = 0$, not 12, so 0 cannot be the answer.
You treated dividing by 0 like dividing by 1. But $12 \times 0 = 0$, not 12.
The outputs grow as the input shrinks, but no number times 0 gives 12. So there is no output at all.

hints.text: Dividing 12 by a number asks: what times that number gives 12?
For input 0: what times 0 gives 12?
Every number times 0 is 0, never 12. So $12 \div 0$ has no answer.

feedback.correct: No number times 0 gives 12, so the machine has no output.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what number times 0 would give 12.

explain.text: A division asks what times 0 gives 12. No number does, so 0 cannot go into this machine. Some inputs are simply not allowed.

screens.prose: This machine is $f(x) = x^2$, but it only accepts inputs from −2 to 3. Drag the point along the whole curve and watch its height, the output.
screens.question: Leave the point where the output is smallest.

hints.text: Watch the height of the point as you drag. Where is it lowest?
The curve dips between the two ends.
At $x = 0$ the height is $0^2 = 0$.

feedback.correct: The lowest point is $(0, 0)$, in the middle of the curve.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the lowest height anywhere on the curve.

byKey.left-end: You stopped at the left end, $x = -2$, where the output is 4. The curve dips lower in the middle.
byKey.right-end: You went to the right end, where the output is 9, the largest. We want the smallest.
byKey.p: The point is not at the bottom of the dip yet. Keep dragging until the height stops falling.

explain.text: The lowest point is at $x = 0$, height 0, in the middle of the curve. The ends give 4 and 9. So the outputs run from 0 up to 9.

screens.prose: The inputs a function accepts are its **domain**. The outputs it gives are its **range**. That curve has domain $-2 \le x \le 3$. The band between the two points shows a range.
screens.question: Drag the two points to the ends of the range of $f(x) = x^2$ on that domain.

hints.text: The range is the set of heights the curve reaches.
The lowest height is where you left the point.
The heights run from 0, at $x = 0$, up to 9, at $x = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark the lowest and highest heights of the curve.

byKey.domain: You marked −2, the left end of the domain. The range is about outputs, the heights on the curve.
byKey.ends: You used $f(-2) = 4$ as the lowest output. The curve dips to 0 at $x = 0$.
byKey.lo: Your lowest point is off. The smallest height on the curve is 0.
byKey.hi: Your highest point is off. The tallest point of the curve is $f(3) = 9$.

explain.text: The range is $0 \le f(x) \le 9$. Its ends are the lowest and highest outputs, not the outputs at the ends of the domain. Filled dots mean 0 and 9 are both reached.

screens.prose: Now the rule itself shuts an input out. $g(x) = \dfrac{12}{x - 2}$.
screens.question: Drag the point to the one input $g$ cannot take.

hints.text: Which input makes the bottom of the fraction zero?
Solve $x - 2 = 0$.
$x = 2$ gives $\dfrac{12}{0}$, which has no answer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the bottom, $x - 2$, is zero.

byKey.zero: You found where $x$ is 0. But the bottom is $x - 2$, which is −2 there. It is 0 at $x = 2$.
byKey.minus-two: At $x = -2$ the bottom is −4, which is fine. The bottom is 0 when $x = 2$.
byKey.p: At that input the bottom, $x - 2$, is not zero, so $g$ works there.

explain.text: At $x = 2$ the bottom is 0 and the machine has no output. Every other number works. The domain is every number except 2, written $x \ne 2$.

screens.prose: $f(x) = 10 - x$, with domain $3 \le x \le 8$, shown by the band. Drag the two points to the ends of the range.
screens.question: Where are the lowest and highest outputs?

hints.text: Work out $f$ at both ends of the domain.
The outputs run from 2 up to 7, so the range is $2 \le f(x) \le 7$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Feed both ends of the domain into $10 - x$.

byKey.reversed: A point sits at 7. If it is your lowest, that is the highest output: bigger inputs give smaller outputs here.
byKey.copied: You copied the domain onto the range. Outputs are $10 - x$, not $x$.
byKey.lo: Your lowest output is off. The biggest input, 8, gives the smallest output.
byKey.hi: Your highest output is off. The smallest input, 3, gives the biggest output.

explain.text: Bigger inputs give smaller outputs here, so $f(8) = 2$ is the lowest and $f(3) = 7$ the highest. The range is $2 \le f(x) \le 7$. Write a range from smallest to largest.

screens.prose: $f(x) = x^2$ again, now with domain $-3 < x \le 2$. The hollow dot at −3 means −3 itself is left out.
screens.question: What is the range?

options.why: You worked out the outputs at the two ends only. $x = 0$ is in the domain and gives 0.
Only $x = -3$ or $x = 3$ give 9, and neither is in the domain. Outputs get close to 9 but never reach it.
You used the right end, $x = 2$, as the top. Inputs near −3 give outputs near 9.

hints.text: Which input in the domain gives the smallest output?
The hollow dot at −3 means −3 is left out, though −2.9 is allowed.
$x = 0$ gives 0. Inputs near −3 give outputs near 9, but never 9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest output, then ask whether 9 is reached.

explain.text: The smallest output is $0^2 = 0$. As $x$ creeps towards −3, $x^2$ creeps towards 9 without reaching it. So the range is $0 \le f(x) < 9$, with a hollow end at 9.

screens.prose: $f(x) = x^2 + 1$, and any number may go in. A colleague says that since every input is allowed, every output is possible too.
screens.question: Can $f(x)$ ever equal 0?

options.why: You squared −1 and got −1. In fact $(-1)^2 = 1$, so $f(-1) = 2$.

options.text: Yes: every number can go in, so every number can come out
options.why: You copied the domain onto the range. Inputs can be anything, but $x^2 + 1$ is never below 1.

hints.text: Can a square be negative?
The lowest point of the curve is $(0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: A square is never negative, so the output is at least 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the lowest point of the curve.

byKey.all: You assumed the range matches the domain. The domain is every number, but the outputs never drop below 1.

explain.text: A square is never negative, so $x^2 + 1$ is at least 1. The domain is every number, but the range is only $f(x) \ge 1$. Domain and range are separate questions.

screens.prose: You found both sets each time. The **domain** is every input allowed, by the rule or by the setting. The **range** is every output those inputs produce. On a number line a filled dot includes its end and a hollow dot leaves it out: $$-3 < x \le 2$$
screens.question: $f(x) = 5x$ has domain $1 \le x \le 4$. What is its range?

options.why: You copied the domain. The outputs are 5 times the inputs.
$x = 0$ is not in the domain, so 0 is not an output.

hints.text: Feed the two ends of the domain into the rule.
$f(1) = 5$ and $f(4) = 20$, and $5x$ climbs steadily between them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The range is made of outputs.

explain.text: $5x$ climbs steadily, so the smallest output comes from the smallest input and the largest from the largest. $f(1) = 5$ and $f(4) = 20$. Both ends are filled, so both are reached.

screens.prose: A put option with strike £100.00 pays $100 - S$ pounds when the final share price $S$ is below £100.00, and nothing otherwise. The payoff is a function of $S$, with domain $S \ge 0$.
screens.question: What is the range of the payoff?

options.why: You treated it like a call. This put pays most when $S$ is 0, and then it pays £100.00.
You read the right end of the price axis. 150 is an input, a final price, not a payoff.
The payoff is never negative. Above £100.00 it pays nothing, which is £0.00.

hints.text: When does the put pay the most?
The line is highest at $S = 0$.
At $S = 0$ it pays £100.00. From £100.00 upwards it pays £0.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the heights of the line, not the prices along the bottom.

explain.text: The payoff is largest, £100.00, when the share is worth nothing. It falls to £0.00 at £100.00 and stays there. So the range is $0 \le \text{payoff} \le 100$, while the domain is every price $S \ge 0$.

ideas: The domain is every input allowed; dividing by 0 and the setting can both shut inputs out.
The range is every output the domain produces: find the lowest and highest heights, not just the ends.
A filled dot includes its end and a hollow dot leaves it out.

formula.name: Domain and range
formula.note: The range comes from the outputs, so check the middle of the domain as well as its ends.

summary.trap: Every input allowed does not mean every output possible: $x^2 + 1$ never drops below 1.

quiz.question: Which input is not in the domain?

options.why: At $x = 4$ the bottom is 8, which is fine. The bottom is 0 when $x = -4$.
At $x = 0$ the bottom is 4. It is the bottom that must not be 0, not $x$.

explain.text: Dividing by 0 has no answer, so the bottom must not be 0. $x + 4 = 0$ when $x = -4$. Every other number is in the domain.

options.why: $x = 3$ is left out of the domain, so 5 is never reached.
You copied the domain. The outputs are $2x - 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Feed both ends into the rule and keep their dots.

explain.text: $f(-1) = -3$, and the filled end keeps it. $f(3) = 5$, but 3 is left out, so 5 is too. The range is $-3 \le f(x) < 5$.

quiz.prose: A trade's profit is $P(q) = 0.5q$ pounds, where $q$ is a whole number of shares from 0 to 100.
quiz.question: Which amount is in the range of $P$?

options.why: That needs $q = 20.5$, and you cannot hold half a share.
That needs $q = 120$, beyond the 100 shares allowed.
That needs $q = -10$. The number of shares starts at 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each amount, work out the $q$ it needs.

explain.text: Each amount needs $q = \text{amount} \div 0.5$. Only £37.50 needs a whole number from 0 to 100: $q = 75$. A domain of whole numbers gives a range with gaps.

quiz.prose: $f(x) = x^2$, and any number may go in.
quiz.question: What is the range?

options.why: Squares are never negative, so no negative output appears.
$x = 0$ is allowed, and it gives 0. So 0 is in the range.

feedback.correct: Every output is 0 or more, and 0 itself is reached.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a square can be negative, and whether it can be 0.

explain.text: A square is never negative, and $0^2 = 0$. Any positive number is reached too, for example 9 from $x = 3$. So the range is $f(x) \ge 0$.
